On the last Thursday of every month, the library lent out sounds. You could borrow rain striking a canvas tent, the click of a good suitcase closing, or the noise a crowd makes when the person onstage forgets the words and everybody decides, at once, to help. These came in little gray boxes with brass hinges. There was no deposit, but you had to bring them back on time. People developed strong attachments to sounds they had not known they needed. The library had lost three copies of Someone Else Washing the Dishes.

I worked the Thursday desk. The job mostly involved checking hinges and explaining that no, we could not lend out silence. People were always disappointed by this. They imagined silence would come in an especially handsome box. In fact, the closest thing we had was Snow Falling on a Closed Swimming Pool, which contained, if you listened long enough, the faint ticking of the pool’s broken clock.

One November evening, a woman named Ruth brought in a sound she wanted to donate. She set a biscuit tin on the desk and said, “My kitchen, around four in the afternoon.”

“Anything in particular happening?”

“No,” she said. Then she thought about it. “The refrigerator, I suppose.”

I lifted the lid. There was the refrigerator, with a shallow rattle at the bottom of its hum. A truck went by. Somewhere beyond the kitchen a child said, “Wait, I wasn’t ready,” with the outrage of someone who had been perfectly ready a moment before. A chair scraped. Then came a tiny, regular clicking I couldn’t identify.

“That’s me,” Ruth said. “I was cutting coupons.”

We had a rule against taking sounds that belonged to other people. A kitchen was usually all right, but the child complicated things. I asked if she knew whose voice it was.

“Oh, that’s me too,” she said.

I looked at her.

“I grew up in that house. I bought it when my father moved out. Some afternoons it all gets mixed together.”

I listened again, and this time there was no child. There was a knife being sharpened, and a man clearing his throat after each pass along the steel, as though he had something to say about the result. Ruth leaned over the desk. Neither of us spoke until he put the knife down.

“He never used it after sharpening it,” she said. “He’d put it straight back in the drawer. Then he’d take out a different knife to cut an apple.”

“Why?”

“I asked him once. He told me to mind my own business.”

She laughed, but only after a second, as if giving him a fair chance to say something else.

I explained the other rule about donations: once a sound went into circulation, you couldn’t ask for it back. You could borrow it like anyone else, but there might be a waiting list. Ruth asked who in the world would want her kitchen. I took her over to the returns cart, where a shoebox labeled Upstairs Neighbor Finally Takes His Boots Off was waiting to be shelved. Its borrowing card had six names on it.

“What if I don’t like what somebody hears in it?” she asked.

I told her about a man who had borrowed Wind in a Pear Tree and brought it back furious because there was a bee. Nobody on staff could hear the bee. He’d grown up picking pears and could tell by the sound which side of the tree it was on. The next borrower was a woman who heard nothing but wind and kept the box open while she did her taxes. She returned it with a note asking us to thank whoever had planted the tree.

Ruth took the tin home. I thought that was the end of it, but she came back just before closing the following month. She had sold the house. The new owners were going to knock down the wall between the kitchen and the dining room, which she admitted was a sensible thing to do. For forty years, anyone carrying a roast to the table had needed another person to hold the door.

“But they’ll never know to ask,” she said, and slid the tin across the desk.

I gave her a donation form. Under DESCRIPTION she wrote Kitchen, 4 p.m. Under CONDITION she wrote Depends. Then she crossed that out and wrote Good.

The first person to borrow the kitchen was a young man who said he was looking for something to play for his dog while he was at work. I nearly told him the sound was too valuable for that. Instead I asked what kind of dog he had. A very old one, he said. Mostly deaf, but not entirely.

When he returned the tin, I asked how it had gone. He said the dog had shown no particular interest. He himself had started coming home for lunch. He would sit on the floor with the dog and eat a sandwich, and afterward he’d have to pick crumbs out of the dog’s coat. He said this as if it were a minor inconvenience that could not easily be resolved.

Ruth’s name went onto the waiting list in February. By the time her turn came, she had moved into an apartment with a refrigerator she described as ostentatiously quiet. I offered to find her a room where she could listen. She said she had groceries in the car, but she sat down anyway, right there at the desk, and opened the tin.

For a while I could hear only the people in the library: a zipper, a cough, the little slap of a picture book hitting the carpet. Then, from somewhere inside the tin, came a knock. Ruth looked up.

“That’ll be Mrs. Flynn,” she said. “She never could work the latch.”

She put one hand flat on the desk and started to get up. Then she remembered where she was. Neither of us moved for a moment. The knock came again, a little louder this time, and Ruth, still half out of her chair, called, “Come in, for heaven’s sake. It’s open.”
